newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK clamps down on electrical goods pricing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK clamps down on electrical goods pricing.

text.p: government said on Wednesday it planned to scrap the system of manufacturers' recommended retail prices for electrical goods to increase competition and secure lower prices for consumers.
But key electricals suppliers criticised the proposals and Britain's biggest electricals retailer Dixons Group Plc said the ban would not affect its pricing policies.

Trade minister Margaret Beckett unveiled a package of measures to stop suppliers and retailers of electrical equipment such as hi-fi systems, televisions, washing machines and fridges, from using recommended prices.

She said an investigation by competition watchdog the Monopolies and Mergers Commission had found that the recommended retail prices had stifled competition and kept prices higher than they otherwise would have been.
"As a result consumers have to pay more than they should," she said in a statement.
The minister said the abolition of recommended prices plus other remedies would mean stronger price competition and more choice of retail outlets.
Shares in Dixons and Kingfisher Plc, the number two player in the British electricals retail market, were up after the government's decision was published.
Dixons' stock was 21.5 pence higher at 592.5 pence, and Kingfisher stood 26 pence higher at 705.

Retail analysts said the shares, which were ahead when the news was released, had dropped back from their highs initially, but then recovered when it became clear the report contained no surprises. The MMC was asked to investigate the electrical goods market back in April 1995. The Commission's recommendation to scrap the retail price pact was leaked the end of May, when The Economist newspaper carried a report saying the MMC favoured abolition.
Beckett also decided to crack down on suppliers' discriminating against certain retailers, including discount warehouse clubs.
She said interested parties had until October 17 to comment on her proposals.
Dixons said the recommended retail price ban had been widely anticipated.
"The recommendations will not affect Dixons Group's long established policy of offering the keenest prices," the company said in a statement.

Earlier this month Dixons chief executive John Clare predicted that if recommended prices were banned it would have no impact on Dixons. But if there were to be a price war the losers would likely be the smaller independents.
Panasonic, one of the suppliers, disagreed with the MMC's conclusion that scrapping recommended prices would benefit consumers, arguing that this might even mean higher prices.
Peter Hamblin, deputy managing director of Panasonic UK predicted shoppers could suffer from the removal of recommended prices from which to negotiate a discount.

"The MMC appears to have reached its conclusions based on the highly selective use of evidence," he said in a statement, which described the MMC study as "fundamentally flawed." -- London Newsroom + 44 171 542 7717
